# Introduction
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is reshaping the global job market, creating both opportunities and challenges for workers across industries. AI-driven automation has transformed routine and repetitive tasks, freeing resources for innovation while also raising concerns about job displacement in traditional roles. At the same time, demand for AI specialists, data scientists, and machine learning engineers has surged, making AI-related careers some of the most sought-after and better-compensated professions today. Understanding how salary trends differ between AI and non-AI careers is therefore essential for evaluating the broader economic impact of technological change.

---

## Research Rationale
The rise of AI is reshaping the labor market, but students entering the job market still face uncertainty about how much AI skills actually affect pay, where the best-paying roles are located, and whether remote jobs offer a true financial advantage. For our team, three students preparing to graduate, this topic is directly tied to our own career decisions. We want to understand how to differentiate ourselves with AI-related skills and titles (e.g., data analyst, machine learning engineer, prompt engineer) in ways that concretely improve salary and employability, not just “sound good” on a résumé.
In 2024, multiple reports show that job postings mentioning AI skills offer sizable salary premiums compared to similar roles without AI, often 20–30% higher pay across industries. At the same time, salary surveys for data science and AI professionals highlight strong but uneven wage growth depending on job title, seniority, and industry. Remote work trends add another layer: recent U.S. studies find that remote workers historically earned a wage premium, but post-pandemic wage growth for remote roles has in some cases been slower than for in-person jobs, which may change how attractive remote work really is from a compensation standpoint.
These trends make salary and compensation a crucial area of study in 2024. Organizations are racing to hire AI-skilled talent, some industries are seeing rapid wage increases (especially in automation and engineering roles), and regional and political differences (e.g., “red vs. blue” states) still shape the gender and skills wage gaps. Understanding how AI vs. non-AI careers compare across regions, work arrangements, and industries will help us: (1) choose roles and locations strategically, (2) prioritize specific AI skills that command the largest premiums, and (3) build a realistic, data-driven career plan rather than relying on hype or anecdotes.

---

## Research Questions & Expected Findings

**Research Questions**

- How do salaries differ across AI vs. non-AI careers?
- What regions offer the highest-paying jobs in AI-related and traditional careers?
- Are remote jobs better paying than in-office roles?
- What industries saw the biggest wage growth in 2024?

**Expected Findings (Hypotheses)**

AI vs. non-AI salaries

- H1: Roles that explicitly require AI / data / ML skills (e.g., data scientist, ML engineer, AI product manager) will have significantly higher median salaries than comparable non-AI roles in the same broad occupation family (e.g., traditional software engineer, business analyst).
- H2: The AI wage premium will be larger in “non-tech” industries (finance, healthcare, legal, manufacturing) where AI skills are still relatively scarce, consistent with reports that AI skills command higher premiums in traditionally non-technical occupations.

Regional differences

- H3: Coastal tech hubs and large metros (e.g., California, Washington, New York, Massachusetts) will show the highest absolute AI salaries, but some lower-cost regions (e.g., parts of the South or Midwest) will offer strong salary-to-cost-of-living trade-offs.
- H4: States and regions with higher concentrations of STEM and “blue” policy environments may have narrower gender wage gaps in AI jobs than more traditional or “red” states, though this might not eliminate the gap entirely.


Remote vs. in-office pay

- H5: Fully remote AI jobs will not always pay more than in-office roles once we control for occupation and seniority. Recent studies suggest remote jobs historically had a wage premium, but post-pandemic wage growth for remote roles has sometimes lagged behind on-site roles. Bureau of Labor Statistics
- H6: Remote roles may show slightly lower cash pay but compensate through non-wage benefits (flexibility, geographic freedom); your Lightcast data may capture this indirectly through location effects.


Industry wage growth in 2024

- H7: Industries tied to automation, control systems, and advanced manufacturing will show some of the strongest year-over-year wage growth, in line with 2024 salary surveys for engineering and automation professionals. Automation.com
- H8: Highly regulated, high-margin sectors (finance, pharma, healthcare) will show both high AI adoption and strong salary growth for AI-adjacent role
